studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details within the unit “In-Depth Study: Character, Setting, Event, and Point of View.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's writing plan and draft work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] At the school newspaper room, Samir opened a folder containing a chart paired with a short editorial. A note on the cover read “In-Depth Study: Character, Setting, Event, and Point of View,” but the pages inside told one unfinished story. Samir expected the ending to explain everything. Instead, the first scene offered only a quiet choice: return a borrowed object without comment or admit why it had been kept.

[2] The main character rehearsed an apology three times. In the first version, every sentence began with “I.” In the second, the character blamed the confusing rules. In the third, the character named the harm, returned the object, and then stopped talking. The narrator never announced which version was sincere.

[3] Amara noticed that a repeated image—a door left slightly open—appeared before each rehearsal. At first it seemed like background description. By its third appearance, the image could suggest an invitation, an escape, or an unfinished decision. The story gave enough detail to support more than one interpretation but not enough to make every interpretation equally strong.

[4] The final scene ended before the apology was delivered. Samir argued that the missing speech made the character seem afraid; Amara thought the pause showed care. To connect the scene to planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details, each reader had to identify exact language, explain an inference, and account for the detail that made the other reading possible.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 48: planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Reading Lab 48: planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details,” then answer: Draft the planned response about planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details. How will each paragraph use the reading rather than merely mention it?

Deliverable: Grade 4: a complete first draft with source-based development in every body section; write two connected paragraphs.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 48: planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 48: planning an in-depth study with a claim and four details.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
